decisions.title: Adopt the personal workflow guide 1.2 for Fruit Market
decisions.question: Should Fruit Market be run with the workflow guide (one approved package at a time, evidence-based checks, decision records)?
decisions.choice: Yes; one package at a time, starting with Package A.
decisions.rationale: The game is complete but releases were unreviewed and records lived in chat history.

impact.player: None directly; fewer broken releases.
impact.technical: Adds checks, records and a release gate.

decisions.reviewTrigger: If the process costs more time than it saves after three packages.

decisions.title: Package A scope = PLAN-001
decisions.question: What should the first setup package contain?
decisions.choice: One verify command, preview before publishing, short records and an owner brief (PLAN-001).
decisions.rationale: Smallest package that stops unreviewed releases and gives the owner a clear way to try builds.

impact.player: None until a release; protects players from silent breakage.
impact.technical: package.json scripts, CI and deploy workflows, new docs.

approval.evidence: Approve PLAN-001 only, including its listed tests and documentation

decisions.reviewTrigger: Acceptance A4 (owner preview playtest) still pending.

decisions.title: Live deploys only through the manual Deploy workflow after verify
decisions.question: When should the live game change?
decisions.choice: Only when the owner runs Deploy LIVE game and types PUBLISH; it runs verify first and a smoke test after. Never on push.
decisions.rationale: Makes 'a preview is not a release' true for this repository.

impact.player: Updates arrive only after the owner approves them.
impact.technical: deploy-web.yml is manual only.

decisions.cost: RM0; one extra tap per release.

approval.evidence: Approve PLAN-001 only, including its listed tests and documentation

decisions.reviewTrigger: If urgent fixes are delayed because nobody pressed Deploy.

decisions.title: PDF exports with pandoc and the existing Playwright browser
decisions.question: Which tool builds the decision PDFs?
decisions.choice: pandoc (Markdown to HTML) plus the project's existing Playwright Chromium (HTML to PDF). No installs.
decisions.rationale: Both are already available; no new dependency.

impact.player: None.
impact.technical: PDF export runs locally, not in CI.

decisions.reviewTrigger: If pandoc is unavailable on the machine that exports.

decisions.title: Budget interpretation: RM500 per month across all games
decisions.question: How should the RM500 monthly ceiling be applied?
decisions.choice: Treat it as portfolio-wide. Fruit Market's current spend is unknown (hypothesis: Cloudflare Free, or Workers Paid at about USD 5).
decisions.rationale: The workflow guide's conservative default.

impact.player: None.
impact.technical: Paid services need a quote and approval.

decisions.reviewTrigger: When the owner states the Cloudflare plan and other paid accounts.

decisions.title: Preview = separate staging Worker
decisions.question: How should changes be previewed, given that Cloudflare preview and version URLs are not generated for Workers with Durable Objects?
decisions.choice: A separate Worker, fruit-market-staging, with its own rooms, leaderboard and stats, updated by CI after checks pass on main.
decisions.rationale: Closest free option to a per-change preview URL; keeps the live data untouched.

impact.player: None; players never see the preview.
impact.technical: A second Worker and a preview job in CI.
impact.data: Separate storage; preview link is unlisted, not private.

decisions.cost: No new paid service; tiny usage within the existing plan.
decisions.reviewTrigger: If Cloudflare adds preview URLs for Durable Object Workers.

decisions.title: Package B scope = PLAN-002
decisions.question: What should the records package contain?
decisions.choice: Canonical JSON records, generated views (register, changelog, state block, PDFs), a records check in verify, release tagging on Deploy, and migration of existing records.
decisions.rationale: Records were kept by hand in several places with nothing checking that they agreed.

impact.player: None directly; releases become traceable.
impact.technical: New records, a generator and checker script, and a deploy step.

approval.evidence: Approve PLAN-002 only, including its listed tests and documentation

decisions.reviewTrigger: If keeping records costs more than it saves.

decisions.title: Canonical record format: JSON records plus Markdown narrative reports
decisions.question: Where is the single source of truth for decisions and packages?
decisions.choice: JSON files in docs/workflow/records; hand-written REP reports stay as narrative snapshots; Markdown, changelog and PDF views are generated.
decisions.rationale: Node reads JSON without dependencies and the check can be strict. YAML needs a parser; plain Markdown can't be validated; a database is ruled out by the guide.

impact.player: None.
impact.technical: Claude edits the JSON; the owner reads the generated views.

approval.evidence: Approve PLAN-002 only, including its listed tests and documentation

decisions.reviewTrigger: If hand edits to JSON become a frequent source of errors.

decisions.title: Records check runs in verify and CI
decisions.question: Should record disagreements fail the build?
decisions.choice: Yes: npm run verify runs records:check, so CI fails on broken records.
decisions.rationale: Once branch protection is on, broken records can't be merged.

impact.player: None.
impact.technical: verify is about 1 second slower.

approval.evidence: Approve PLAN-002 only, including its listed tests and documentation

decisions.reviewTrigger: If the check blocks urgent fixes for record reasons.

decisions.title: Reconnect fix scope = PLAN-004 (evidence first, then fix)
decisions.question: How should the intermittent rejoin failure be fixed?
decisions.choice: Collect evidence and reproduce it with a stress test before changing game code; fix only the measured root cause, with a regression test.
decisions.rationale: Reading the code didn't identify a certain cause, and two failures in five runs are too rare to debug by guessing. The workflow guide says to reproduce and isolate before fixing.

impact.player: Fewer stuck screens after a reload or dropped connection, once the fix is published.
impact.technical: New stress test and diagnostics; a small fix in the online client or room server.
impact.data: Diagnostics stay in CI artifacts for 7 days; they contain test players only.

decisions.cost: RM0 (GitHub Actions minutes are free for public repositories)

approval.evidence: Approve PLAN-004 only, including its listed tests and documentation

decisions.reviewTrigger: If not reproduced after 300 cycles: stop and report.

decisions.title: Stress test runs on demand, not on every push
decisions.question: Should the long reconnect stress test run in every CI run?
decisions.choice: No: a manual CI workflow plus local runs. Every-push CI keeps the existing tests (about 15 minutes).
decisions.rationale: Hundreds of cycles would make every CI run far slower; the stress test is for investigation and before releases.

impact.player: None.
impact.technical: One extra manual workflow.

approval.evidence: Approve PLAN-004 only, including its listed tests and documentation

decisions.reviewTrigger: If reconnect bugs slip through between releases.

decisions.title: 4-player clarity scope = PLAN-005 (screen text only)
decisions.question: How should the game make 4-player play discoverable?
decisions.choice: Clearer screen text and open-seat rows in the lobby, short hints on the home, quick-match and new-game screens, plus an automated 4-person test. No rule or server changes.
decisions.rationale: 4-player play already works; only discoverability is missing. Text changes are low risk and fast to verify.

impact.player: Groups of 3 or 4 can find how to play together.
impact.technical: src/ui/Online.tsx, src/ui/App.tsx, styles; one new browser test.

approval.evidence: Approve PLAN-005 only, including its listed tests and documentation

decisions.reviewTrigger: If playtesters still miss how to invite more than one friend.

decisions.title: Publish version 1.1.1 to players
decisions.question: Should the 1.1.1 candidate (reconnect fix, 4-player clarity, release process) replace 1.1.0 on the live game?
decisions.choice: Recommended after the owner's 15-minute preview playtest passes. Publication happens only when the owner runs Deploy LIVE game and types PUBLISH.
decisions.rationale: Fixes a bug players can hit (stuck on Connecting after a reload or rejoin) and makes group play discoverable. The game-code change is small (4 files, about 40 lines), the server code is unchanged, and all automated checks pass.

impact.player: Fewer stuck online screens; clearer 2 to 4 player options.
impact.technical: Live Worker updated to the candidate commit and tagged v1.1.1.
impact.data: No data or storage format change; rolling back is safe.

approval.evidence: yes to 1 and 2 (1 = release 1.1.1: approve DEC-013, then the owner presses Deploy LIVE game)

decisions.reviewTrigger: If the preview playtest finds a problem, or the post-deploy smoke test fails.

decisions.title: Use the Concept and Theme Companion for creative work
decisions.question: Should Fruit Market's creative decisions follow the Game Concept and Theme Companion (edition 1.0) alongside the development workflow?
decisions.choice: Yes, with one shared record system (same reports, register and PDFs); creative approval never implies implementation approval.
decisions.rationale: Keeps creative and development decisions in one history and avoids a parallel register.

impact.player: None directly.
impact.technical: None; documentation process only.

decisions.reviewTrigger: If creative work starts needing its own package type.

decisions.title: Adopt three design pillars
decisions.question: Which design pillars guide Fruit Market's creative choices?
decisions.choice: 1) Fresh fruit, fast money. 2) Outprice rivals in secret. 3) A cheerful town market. Each with inclusion and exclusion rules (REP-010 section 3).
decisions.rationale: Derived from the actual rules and the strongest theme-to-mechanic matches found in the review.

impact.player: Future features and content are judged against these.
impact.technical: None now.

approval.evidence: yes to 1 and 2 (2 = approve DEC-015 and DEC-016)

decisions.reviewTrigger: If playtests show players value something the pillars exclude.

decisions.title: First creative test: reveal-comprehension playtest
decisions.question: What is the smallest useful test of the riskiest creative hypothesis?
decisions.choice: 3 to 5 first-time players, Quick game vs 1 computer shop, no coaching; continue if at least 3 of 4 can explain a lost sale by day 3 (provisional, owner-set). No code.
decisions.rationale: Pillar 2 depends on players understanding why they won or lost a sale; no player evidence exists yet.

impact.player: Testers play the existing game.
impact.technical: None.
impact.data: Notes only; no personal data kept.

approval.evidence: yes to 1 and 2 (2 = approve DEC-015 and DEC-016)

decisions.reviewTrigger: After the first playtest round.

decisions.title: Setting: a market where the whole world shops
decisions.question: Where is Fruit Market's market?
decisions.choice: Option C: a deliberate 'the whole world shops here' mix. A sunny harbour market; customers from every culture and fantasy role; seaside palette; plain market dollars.
decisions.rationale: Keeps the existing art and cast, turns the mix into an intentional identity, and costs nothing now.

impact.player: No visible change now; guides future content.
impact.technical: None now; recorded in the creative bible.

approval.evidence: 1. Where is this market? C: a deliberate “the whole world shops here” mix.

decisions.reviewTrigger: If playtesters find the setting confusing.

decisions.title: Rename Panda Lim while keeping the cast coherent
decisions.question: Should the 'Panda Lim' rival be renamed?
decisions.choice: Yes: an animal nickname that fits beside Foxy Rosa, Big Benny, Uncle Toad, Rocky and Pinky; picture and lines unchanged. Cast rules recorded in the creative bible.
decisions.rationale: Avoids pairing a surname with a national symbol while preserving the animal-trader theme.

impact.player: New games show the new name.
impact.technical: One data line plus tests (PLAN-006).
impact.data: Saved games keep the old name until they end.

approval.evidence: Rename Panda Lim? - sure, but dont run away from the general theme coherence

decisions.reviewTrigger: If the new name tests poorly with players.

decisions.title: Rename scope = PLAN-006, shipped in 1.1.2
decisions.question: How and when should the rename be built?
decisions.choice: As PLAN-006 (display name, reserved names, compatibility tests), released as 1.1.2 after 1.1.1 is live.
decisions.rationale: Keeps the 1.1.1 candidate unchanged; the rename is small and safe but still needs its own checks.

impact.player: New name from 1.1.2.
impact.technical: Small data change plus tests.

approval.evidence: Approve PLAN-006 only, including its listed tests and documentation, name: Patches

decisions.reviewTrigger: If 1.1.1 is delayed for long.

decisions.title: UI and UX polish in three phases
decisions.question: How should the game's look and feel be made to feel finished?
decisions.choice: Phase 1 fixes 9 visible defects (PLAN-007, ships in 1.1.2); phase 2 calms the table layout and phase 3 adds a design system, motion and sound, both designed as phone-viewable mockups first (PLAN-008) and built only after the owner picks; playtest before and after.
decisions.rationale: The review found concrete causes (defects, clutter, no focus, inconsistent system). Fixing defects is cheap and safe; layout changes need the owner's eye and player evidence.

impact.player: A cleaner, clearer game in steps.
impact.technical: Presentation code only; no rules, saves or server.

decisions.reviewTrigger: If the baseline playtest shows a different priority.

decisions.title: Art direction: B, toy-box tabletop
decisions.question: Which art direction should the polish follow, given the owner dislikes the current art style and points to It Takes Two?
decisions.choice: Direction B: a smooth 2D toy-like tabletop style (rounded shapes, wood, felt and clay materials, warm light, soft shadows, motion on every action), drawn by Claude as vector art; a paid illustrator stays a later, separately priced option. The A/B/C style test is dropped.
decisions.rationale: B addresses clutter, feel and art style, keeps phones fast and costs nothing to test; C is too large and risky now; A does not answer the art-style concern.

impact.player: A warmer, toy-like look with more motion, if chosen and built.
impact.technical: Redraw of fruits, about 30 characters, rivals, about 40 icons and the UI (only after approval of a build plan).

decisions.cost: RM0 for the test; any illustrator needs a quote and approval
decisions.reviewTrigger: After the style test, or if the owner wants a paid illustrator.

decisions.title: Look and tone: cunning edition of direction B
decisions.question: How should direction B reflect the game's undercutting mechanic?
decisions.choice: Keep the toy-box tabletop style and add a cheeky, scheming layer: plum and gold for secret moments (pricing, reveal, evening), wax-sealed face-down price boards, 'Psst' whisper bubbles that restate public facts, sly rival faces (Foxy Rosa winks), a spotlight reveal with an 'Outfoxed by $1!' headline, and the tagline 'Undercut. Outfox. Sell it fresh.'
decisions.rationale: The owner asked for the look to match the undercut mechanic. Cheeky rather than mean keeps pillar 3 (a cheerful town market) and pillar 2 (outprice rivals in secret) aligned; the market stays sunny by day.

impact.player: Secret phases feel secret and the reveal feels like a showdown, if built.
impact.technical: Same redraw as DEC-021 plus a plum secret-phase theme; only after a build plan is approved.
impact.data: None. Whispers only restate information the game already shows; no hidden prices or choices.

approval.evidence: yes but align more with the cunning aesthetic given the undercut mechanism of the game

decisions.reviewTrigger: If playtesters read the rivals as mean, or the plum screens feel too dark.

decisions.title: Look: cosy pixel edition of direction B
decisions.question: The cunning edition lost the cosy feel and the toy-box art moved too far from pixel art. What should the look be?
decisions.choice: Go back to the first toy-box mockups (warm cream, teal and wood; the owner's own Evening layout edit) and use the game's own pixel characters, fruit and icons with its pixel heading font, inside the smooth, polished frame. Keep a light sly touch in warm colours: dotted 'Psst' whispers from Foxy Rosa, a sly-eyed Foxy Rosa and Patches, sealed prices, 'Outfoxed by $1!'. Drop the dark plum screens, curtain and spotlight.
decisions.rationale: Owner feedback: the first toy-box version felt cosy; the cunning edition did not; balance the art back toward pixel art. Reusing the game's sprites also means far less redraw work than a full vector cast.

impact.player: Familiar pixel cast and fruit, cleaner screens, cosy warm colours, if built.
impact.technical: Much smaller art job than DEC-021: reuse and tidy the existing sprites; the UI frame is the main build.
impact.data: None. Whispers repeat only public information.

decisions.reviewTrigger: Owner review of the cosy pixel mockups; if confirmed, DEC-022's plum layer is superseded.

decisions.title: Layout: one shared market table (board game, not menus)
decisions.question: The cosy pixel mockups still felt like menus. How should the game screens be laid out?
decisions.choice: Every game screen is the same market table, like the current game: customers queue along the street at the top, Foxy Rosa's and Patches' stalls flank the market in the middle, your stall sits at the bottom. Pricing seals boards on each stall; the reveal flips the boards on the stalls themselves, the winner's stall glows, coins fly to it and the customer walks over; at night the stalls light lanterns and the market is covered. Keeps DEC-023's pixel art, warm colours and smooth buttons.
decisions.rationale: Owner: "revamp the current UI/UX to match the cosiness of the previous UI/UX board layout" and "the one currently feels very menu based, instead of board game". Seeing everyone at one table is what made the current game feel cosy.

impact.player: The game feels like a board game you sit at, with less clutter than today.
impact.technical: Reuses the current game's table structure; the build restyles it rather than replacing it.
impact.data: None. Rival boards stay sealed until the bell; whispers repeat only public information.

decisions.reviewTrigger: Owner review of the table mockups.
